title: 4-Day Silent Retreat of Seven Meditations – Peace Temple Retreats
excerpt: Thursday, July 4 - Sunday, July 7 REGISTER       Re-align and connect, let go, refocus and dive deeper into meditation practice whether you are beginner or an experienced practitioner. Throughout the weekend we share multiple meditation practices rooting in Tibetan, Indian and Thai traditions. Please prepare to spend much of the weekend in noble silence to get the most out of your practice.  Recharge in the sauna, swim in the pond, enjoy nature walks and take in the sun, while our chef prepares a delicious selection of healthy meals to complement your rejuvenating experience at Peace Temple.   Who this retreat is for     	Anyone who is curious about meditation and breath-work  	Anyone curious about different traditions of buddhism  	Anyone who feels anxiety and wants to learn methods to work with it  	Anyone who feels the time has come for devices / media detox  	Anyone who wants to spend the weekend diving into themselves, and diving into the pond!        So join us in quieting the mind so you can hear your heart, while detoxing in sauna, having hearty vegan meals in a stunning natural environment.   Retreat schedule  Thursday    	3:00pm - 7:00pm - Arrival  	7:00 - 8:00 pm - Dinner  	8:00 - 9:00 pm - Welcome circle around the fire  	9:00 - 9:30 pm - Elements meditation  	10:00 pm - Rest   Friday    	9:00 - 10:00 am - Gentle movement and loving kindness meditation  	10:00 - 11:00 am - Breakfast  	11:00 - 12:00 pm - Silent time in nature  	12:00 - 12:30 pm - Dharma talk  	12:30 - 1:30 pm - Guided meditation practice  	1:30 - 2:30 pm - Lunch  	2:30 - 3:30 pm - Walking meditation  	3:30 - 4:00 pm - Dharma talk  	4:00 - 5:00 pm - Anapana (Guided breath meditation)  	5:00 - 6:30 pm - Sauna and swimming  	7:00 - 8:00 pm - Dinner  	8:00 - 8:30 pm - Questions and Answers (With notes instead of talking)  	8:30 - 9:00 pm - Elements meditation  	9:00 - 10:00 pm - Gong sound bath and loving kindness meditation  	10:00 pm - Rest   Saturday    	9:00 - 10:00 am - Gentle movement and loving kindness meditation  	10:00 - 11:00 am - Breakfast  	11:00 - 12:00 pm - Silent time in nature  	12:00 - 12:30 pm - Dharma talk  	12:30 - 1:30 pm - Guided meditation practice  	1:30 - 2:30 pm - Lunch  	2:30 - 3:30 pm - Walking meditation  	3:30 - 4:00 pm - Dharma talk  	4:00 - 5:00 pm - Anapana (Guided breath meditation)  	5:00 - 6:30 pm - Sauna and swimming  	7:00 - 8:00 pm - Dinner  	8:00 - 8:30 pm - Questions and Answers (With notes instead of talking)  	8:30 - 9:00 pm - Elements meditation  	9:00 - 10:00 pm - Gong sound bath and loving kindness meditation  	10:00 pm - Rest   Sunday    	10:00 - 11:00 am - Breakfast  	11:00 - 11:30 pm - Dharma Talk  	11:30 - 12:30 pm - Active Meditation Practice  	12:30 - 1:30 pm - Vipassana meditation (Mindfulness of the body)  	1:30 - 2:30 pm - Lunch  	2:30 - 3:30 pm - Walking meditation  	3:30 - 4:30 pm - Closing sharing circle with loving kindness meditation  	4:30 pm - Departure    Facilitators       Olga Klimova started practicing meditation in 2008 in the tradition of U Ba Khin and S.N. Goenka. She learned Anapana, Vipassana and Metta meditation techniques and attended and did service for many retreats in this tradition over the years. Olga has been following the Buddhist path to awakening very diligently, practicing sitting meditation several hours each day for many years, with the basis of the most fundamental principles of sila (5 precepts), which is essential for achieving good samadhi (mind concentration).  Four years ago Olga connected with the monastics in Theravada Buddhist tradition and discovered a large library of books and Dhamma talks explaining the path to awakening from perspectives renounced teachers of advanced monastic practitioners.  Recently Olga traveled to Thailand, a Buddhist country that preserved the Dhamma knowledge and wisdom very well, and is also is a home to many monasteries and enlightened teachers. Olga spent time in a monastery in Thailand, Wat Marp Jan, studying with monastics and learning their way in order to dive deeper into the meditation practice.  Olga has a close connection with the Empty Cloud monastery in New Jersey, whose abbot, Bhante Suddhaso (who has been in robes for 20 years), became a true friend and a guide in a more advanced meditation practice.  Vladimir Kuperman started practicing meditation in 2006 after returning from a transformational trip to Ladakh, a small country bordering Tibet in the Himalayan Mountains, and  heartfelt teaching of the Dalai Lama in the northern India.  Vladimir has attended New York Insight Meditation center for many years while living in NYC, learning breath concentration meditation along with walking meditation and loving kindness meditation from many prominent teachers. There he also learned the importance of Sangha - a spiritual community that supports each others path.  Vladimir's meditation practice played an integral role in establishment of Peace Temple - a spiritual retreat center in the beautiful Catskill Mountains, devoted to creating and holding peaceful and inspiring community events, where creativity, spiritual growth, sustainability, respect for nature, and respect for each other are practiced.  Besides hosting the retreat, Vladimir will lead morning yoga, loving kindness (Meta) meditation and Walking meditation from Theravada Buddhist tradition. In addition, Vladimir will lead sound bath sessions, nature hike and facilitate Central American Sauna. Since the emergence of positive psychology, the study of character strengths has been at the forefront of research into human well-being and optimal functioning. Originally developed to provide the field with a solid base for research on what enables and promotes good character and the good life (Peterson and Seligman, 2004), the character strength and virtue classification is now considered one of the main building blocks of positive psychology. It identifies 24 strengths that act as the psychological mechanisms defining virtues, categorized into six overarching groups: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance, and transcendence.

Character strengths are the positive parts of our personality that make us feel authentic and engaged. They are a core and foundational part of who we are and govern our development, wellbeing, and life satisfaction (Niemiec, 2013). They influence how we think, act, feel, and represent what we value in ourselves and others. Research shows that by drawing on our strengths, we can have a more influential positive impact on others, improve our relationships, and enhance our wellbeing and happiness.

The most widespread measure of character strengths is the Values in Action Inventory of Strengths (VIA-IS), which has been administered to over 13,000,000 individuals worldwide (Littman-Ovadia et al., 2021). Everyone possesses all 24 character strengths to different degrees, so each person has a truly unique character strengths profile. Understanding how each sits within our personal capacity therefore allows us to respond and behave in more positive ways.

We went to all of these places between August 17th and September 4th of last year, which was a really nice time of year to go.  Road tripping made for an awesome way to see some of the famous sights in Northern California and the Pacific Northwest, and to hit a lot of great trails and campgrounds as well. But the best part is that there are also a ton of hidden gems to explore along the way, outside of the parks. It’s a beautiful drive the whole way, too.  Our itinerary, including the five highlights mentioned in this reel, looked something like this:  California: -Yosemite -Lake Tahoe -Lassen Volcanic National Park -Burney Falls -Mount Shasta  Oregon: -Klamath Falls Area -Crater Lake -Bend Area -Canon Beach/OR Coast -Trillium Lake/Mt. Hood -Hood River -Multnomah Falls/Portland  Washington: -Mount Rainier -Alpine Lakes Wilderness -North Cascades  -Mt. Baker  It’s probably 20 plus hours of total driving to do this whole trip, which is why I’d recommend 3 weeks or more if possible. If you don’t mind tacking on a little more, it’s also worth driving out to Redwood National Park in Northern California, and Olympic National Park in between visiting Rainier and the North Cascades. A specialized room where NIST researchers can make acoustical measurements without an echo.  All six sides (including top and bottom) of the room are covered in fiberglass wedges that absorb sound with the bottom floor covered by an additional layer of wires suspended a few feet in the air. This is where electroacoustic devices, such as microphones, loudspeakers and hearing aids, are measured.  The room is surrounded by concrete walls that are 0.3 meters thick and sits on 52 coil springs to reduce vibrations from the outside.  Because of these features, sound that is generated inside the room gets absorbed by the walls. There’s practically no echo or reverb down to 45 hertz and the wedges absorb 99 percent of the sound that hits them.  Another aspect of the room design is that sound from outside stays outside (which explains how quiet it can get in here!).  NIST researchers use this chamber for research towards developing documentary standards – official ways to specify test methods or procedures - for hearing aids. One example includes standardized procedures for measuring the directivity index, a parameter that is commonly used to characterize the performance of directional hearing aids.
